text: Prefix hashes, double modulus.

String hashing (字符串哈希) turns a string into a number: h(s) = s1·Bn−1 + … + sn (mod M). With prefix hashes h[i] and powers p[i], the hash of any substring s[l..r] is h[r] − h[l−1]·p[r−l+1], in O(1). Equal strings always have equal hashes; different strings collide only rarely.

Use two moduli (or one 61-bit modulus) to make collisions practically impossible. Hashing + binary search answers "longest common prefix of two substrings" in O(log n), which already solves many suffix- array problems more slowly but more simply.
abc aaaa abc abcc
How many different strings (P3370): hash each, sort the pairs, count distinct. O(total length + n log n).
Base B larger than the alphabet (131, 13331), moduli prime. On Codeforces, fixed bases can be attacked by hacks; pick B at random at run time there.
The match box; the mirror palindrome.

The Z-function (Z 函数 , 扩展 KMP): z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i..]. Keep the rightmost match box [l, r): inside it, z[i] starts from min(r − i, z[i − l]), then extend by comparing characters. Every comparison either fails once or moves r right: O(n).
To match b against a, compute the Z-function of b, then run the same loop over a using b's z values (P5410). Z and KMP's nxt carry the same information; use whichever feels natural.
aaaabaa aaaaa
Inside the box, a[i..] looks like b[i − l..], whose answer z[i − l] is known; it is only trusted up to the end of the box r. Beyond r we compare by hand.
Classic uses: all occurrences of b in a (ext[i] == m); the shortest period; checking which prefixes are also suffixes.

Manacher (马拉车) finds the longest palindrome around every centre in O(n). Insert a separator between characters (#a#b#a#) so even and odd palindromes look the same. Keep the palindrome reaching furthest right, centre c, right end r: a centre i < r starts from the radius of its mirror 2c − i, capped by r − i, then extends.
aaa
babad
cbbd
With separators, a radius p[i] in t is exactly the length of the palindrome in the original string. The different end characters ^ and $ stop the extension without index checks (P3805).

Longest double palindrome (P4555): for each separator, the longest palindrome ending there plus the longest starting there, both read off p[]. Counting palindromes = Σ ⌈p[i] / 2⌉ over the right centres.
Doubling with counting sort; height by Kasai.

The suffix array (后缀数组) lists the starting positions of all suffixes in sorted order. Build it by doubling: sort by the first 1, 2, 4, … characters, using the ranks from the previous round as pairs (rank of i, rank of i + k). With counting sort each round is O(n): O(n log n) total (P3809).

The height (LCP) array: height[i] = lcp of the suffixes at sorted positions i − 1 and i. Kasai's trick computes it in O(n): going through suffixes in text order, the lcp drops by at most 1 each step. Number of distinct substrings = n(n + 1)/2 − Σ height (P2408).

Each round sorts by (rank[i], rank[i + k]) with two counting sorts: first by the second key (suffixes with no second half come first), then stably by the first key. Stop early when all ranks are different.

Height answers lcp questions: lcp of any two suffixes = minimum of height between their sorted positions (with an ST table, 第3章). Longest substring occurring ≥ k times (P2852) = the best minimum over k − 1 consecutive heights.
States, links, clones; counting with the link tree.

The suffix automaton (后缀自动机 , SAM) is the smallest automaton accepting exactly the substrings of s, with at most 2n states. Each state is a class of substrings with the same set of end positions; len[v] = the longest of them, link[v] = the state of the longest suffix in a different class. Built online, one character at a time, in amortised O(n).

Each state v contains substrings of lengths len[link[v]] + 1 … len[v], so distinct substrings = Σ (len[v] − len[link[v]]). The suffix links form a tree; the number of occurrences of a state = number of prefix-end states in its link subtree.
abab
P3804 asks for the largest (occurrences × length) over substrings occurring more than once: "ab" occurs twice, 2 × 2 = 4. "abab" has 7 distinct substrings: a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab.

The clone step is the part everyone gets wrong: the clone copies q's transitions and link, takes len = len[p] + 1, gets no occurrence count of its own, and both q and cur then link to it. Size the arrays as 2n states.

Which structure? Hashing for quick equality tests; Z / KMP for one pattern; Manacher for palindromes; AC automaton for many patterns; suffix array for sorted suffixes and lcp ranges; SAM for counting substrings and occurrences online (生成魔咒 P4070 adds characters one by one).
